newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ budget surplus seen only half earlier forecast.
newsitem.headline: NZ budget surplus seen only half earlier forecast.

text.p: New Zealand Treasurer Winston Peters on Thursday will table his first budget showing a surplus only half the NZ$3.3 billion (US$2,26 billion) forecast in March, government sources said on Tuesday.
In the past week Peters and other senior government ministers have been warning the 1997/98 surplus would be lower than recent forecasts.
Other insiders have let slip that the surplus will be as low as half the previous forecast.

Ministers blame slower growth, higher debt servicing costs, and the one-off effects of lower surpluses from state-owned companies, technical changes and a NZ$200 million settlement of historical greivances of South Island Maori.
"The total effect of these changes in tax and expenditure means there will be a reduction in the level of surplus for 1997/98 compared to previous forecasts," Peters told the House on Thursday.
But he said there would still be a large enough buffer if the economy or other events proved less favourable than current forecasts.

One government source said the surplus would be about double the first surplus of the 1990s - NZ$755 million in 1994 - but would not be below NZ$1.5 billion. Others suggested a figure of between NZ$1.5 billion and NZ$1.7 billion.
But it would not be unusual for the government to send signals which were too pessimistic to reap the public relations benefits of a better outcome on budget day.

A survey by Standard and Poor's (mostly taken before ministers' warnings of a lower surplus) showed economists expected the budget to forecast a 1997/98 surplus of NZ$2.6 billion, although they foresaw a final surplus of NZ$2.1 billion.

Standard and Poor's said there was a risk the budget could go into deficit if there was a significant financial shock or forecasting error. It said the Reserve Bank's economic assumptions due on Friday were likely to be more pessimistic.
The average prediction of nine economists surveyed by Reuters was NZ$2.23 billion, but again some replies were received before the government's attempts to lower expectations.
Despite the lower surplus forecasts, Prime Minister Jim Bolger said the economy was bottoming out at more than two percent growth and would rebound in coming years.
Bolger said on Friday the surplus would still be strong and it had to be seen in context.
"New Zealand is one of only three countries in the developed world that produces a surplus and we produced our first surplus only in 1994," Bolger said.

The coalition government has pledged to go ahead with NZ$950 million extra spending in the 1997-1998 year, mainly on health and education, up to NZ$1.7 billion in 1998/99 and NZ$2.35 billion in 1999/2000.

It has also promised to scrap a surtax on pensions in April 1998 so that will not have its full impact in the 1997/98 year. A planned tax cut for middle income earners costing NZ$1.1 billion has been deferred until July 1, 1998 to allow for the extra spending.

The coalition also agreed to put NZ$300 million more a year into capital expenditure, and this is likely to be increased in the budget as the government uses dividends and capital repayments from its trading companies to fund a big rise in the number of new schools and spending on hospitals.
